item.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
item.description: [Open Source Software] Keyword: FOSS — A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

item.title: Why land—a scarce resource—is so important for climate protection
item.description: [Open Source Software] Keyword: FOSS — A new study quantifies, for the first time, the interrelationships and competing objectives of two major areas of action for reducing greenhouse gas emissions: the phaseout of fossil fuels and measures taken on natural land, such as farmland, forests and wetlands. It demonstrates how a well-balanced policy mix can keep costs low for both people and nature. The study, conducted at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK), was published in Nature Sustainability.

item.title: Finding new life in old chemicals for pharmaceuticals using light-driven chemistry
item.description: [Diabetes & Kidney Disease] Keyword: type 2 diabetes — Drug companies maintain large libraries of chemical compounds that can be screened for potential use in the development of new pharmaceuticals. One class of these compounds, sulfonamides, is used in antibiotics and in drugs to treat type 2 diabetes, hypertension and inflammation. Thousands of these sulfonamides exist in these libraries, but their use beyond their initial purpose is limited because they are difficult to chemically modify.

item.title: Mental health app may help unemployed people find jobs, six-week trial suggests
item.description: [Science & Research] Keyword: clinical trial — Losing a job can be a life-shattering experience. And when depression complicates a job search, unemployment can become a vicious cycle. Now, a Northwestern University–led clinical trial suggests a new intervention may break that cycle: a phone app, named DRIVEN, that combines weekly self-guided mental health exercises (to reduce stress and increase motivation) with job-seeking strategies.
